kinds.d: Unique photograph on a silvered copper plate, usually kept in a small folding case; introduced 1839, superseded by c.1856.
Unique positive photograph on glass by the wet collodion process, usually cased; popular mid-1850s to 1860s.
Direct-positive photograph on thin black-lacquered iron sheet, most common in the 1860s and 1870s.
Small portrait photograph mounted on a card about 2.5 by 4 inches, common from the 1860s.

x.d: Disdéri's patented format of several small portraits on one plate, cut and mounted as visiting-card-size prints.
x.dt: photograph 54 × 89 mm on 64 × 100 mm card · studio backmark

kinds.d: Photograph mounted on a card about 4.25 by 6.5 inches, which replaced the carte de visite from the late 1860s.
Two near-identical photographs mounted side by side on a card for viewing in a stereoscope.

x.d: Early commercial stereo cards from the London firm whose principal photographer was William England.
Stereographs from the Underwood brothers' firm, which ended stereo production in 1920.
Educational, comic and sentimental stereoviews from the world's largest stereographic company, made 1892–1963.

kinds.d: Photograph printed on paper or card that is not a snapshot, mounted card format or postcard.
Informal amateur photographic print made with a hand camera, unmounted and usually small.
Photograph developed in or from the camera itself on peel-apart or integral instant film.

x.d: Print separated from its negative after development, from roll film and later pack film.
Self-developing integral print with the white frame, introduced with the SX-70 system.

v.d: films made in the former Enschede factory

x.d: Fujifilm integral instant print in credit-card, square and wide sizes.

kinds.d: Developed transparency mounted for projection or viewing.

x.d: Photograph printed on glass for projection in a magic lantern or stereopticon.
x.dt: size · hand-coloured or plain · paper binding

x.d: 35 mm colour transparency returned from Kodak labs in a 2 × 2 inch cardboard mount.
Cardboard disc holding seven stereo pairs (14 transparencies) for the View-Master viewer.

kinds.d: Developed photographic negative on film or plate.

brands.d: Meadville, Pennsylvania stereoview maker founded by B. L. Singley; world's largest stereographic company by 1905.
Stereograph and news-photo firm of Elmer and Bert Underwood; sold its stereo stock to Keystone in 1921.
London photographic firm of Nottage and Kennard selling stereo cards and photographs; dissolved 1922, name revived 2005.
Edwin Land's instant-photography company; formats and trademarks passed to the Impossible Project, now Polaroid B.V.
Japanese photographic and imaging company, maker of Instax instant film.
Eastman Kodak, the Rochester photographic company that popularised roll-film cameras and colour slide film.
Portland, Oregon photo-finisher that launched the View-Master in 1939; bought by GAF in 1966.

notes: All six old kinds kept ('Other photographs' renamed Photographic print; its RPPC model moved to the Postcards shelf, its CDV/cabinet card/snapshot aliases dropped as they are their own kinds). New kinds Daguerreotype, Ambrotype, Tintype, Stereoview card and Instant print sourced. Old CDV model entry 'Carte de visite' dropped as it only repeated the kind name. View-Master reels kept here as a Slide type/archetype (could cross-link to Toys). Case/plate sizes and studios left as detail; plate-size names not on retrieved pages.
